title: MARS: Hand the Problem to the Right Specialist
hook: Most multi-agent coding pipelines split work into planner, coder, debugger. MARS splits it by algorithmic topic instead — and gets most of the accuracy of a heavier pipeline at a third of the wall-clock cost.
key_points: Standard multi-agent code pipelines use generic roles and leave the choice of algorithmic technique entirely to the backbone model.
MARS instead makes each agent a topic specialist — dynamic programming, graphs, strings, geometry — grounded by RAG over an algorithm-theory corpus.
Retrieval picks a small team of relevant specialists per problem; a starter writes C++17, then each turn tests the draft in a sandbox.
The active specialist may keep, repair, or hand off the draft, forwarding a structured packet to the next specialist; a final pass normalizes boilerplate.
On CodeContests with Gemma 4 it reaches a 0.624 pass rate, +14.4 points over direct prompting, in 2.3 pipeline stages per task.
That trails CodeSIM (0.731) but runs 3.3x cheaper in wall-clock time with much smaller variance in per-task token spend.
content_html: Multi-agent coding pipelines usually cut the work into generic roles — a planner, a coder, a debugger — which means the hard question of which algorithm this problem wants still falls entirely on the backbone model. MARS (Multi-Agent Relay of Specialized LLMs), from Andrei Mikhailov, Mikhail Burtsev and Alsu Sagirova, cuts along a different seam: every agent is a specialist in one algorithmic topic.
extra_html:
How the relay works

Retrieval over an algorithm-theory corpus selects a small team of relevant specialists for the problem at hand. A starter agent writes an initial C++17 solution; each subsequent turn runs the current candidate against the public examples in a sandbox, and the active specialist decides whether to keep it, repair it, or hand it off — passing a structured packet to the next specialist. One infrastructure-fixer pass at the end normalizes boilerplate. The whole thing is prompt-only: no fine-tuning, just routing plus grounding.

What it buys

On the CodeContests test split with Gemma 4, the authors report a 0.624 ± 0.006 pass rate at 2.3 recorded pipeline stages per task — 14.4 percentage points above direct prompting. That doesn't beat CodeSIM (0.731), but it closes most of the gap at 3.3× lower wall-clock cost and with substantially less variance in tokens spent per task. The interesting claim isn't the leaderboard position; it's that what you specialize on matters as much as how many agents you run, and that predictable cost can be worth a few points of accuracy. Code is on GitHub; details and caveats are in the paper.

related.title: AlphaCode: Competition-Level Code Generation
related.hook: Generate a massive pool of candidate programs for competitive-programming problems, filter by test-case behavior, cluster by output, and reach roughly the level of a median human competitor.

related.title: Multi-LCB: Code Eval Beyond Python
related.hook: LiveCodeBench keeps coding evals contamination-free — but only in Python. Multi-LCB extends it to twelve languages and finds models that look strong are quietly overfit to Python.

related.title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective
related.hook: Multi-agent LLM setups help sometimes and hurt other times, with no clear pattern — until you view them as an information bottleneck problem: compressing context helps only when it loses less than it saves.

flashcards.prompt: How does MARS divide labor differently from a typical multi-agent coding pipeline?

choices.text: By algorithmic topic — each agent specializes in DP, graphs, strings, geometry, and so on
By generic role — planner, coder, and debugger agents
By programming language, one agent per target language

flashcards.explanation_html: Generic planner/coder/debugger roles leave technique selection to the backbone model. MARS makes specialization the axis of division and uses retrieval to pick which specialists a problem needs.

flashcards.prompt: What happens on each turn of the MARS relay?
flashcards.back_html: The candidate solution is run against public examples in a sandbox; the active specialist then keeps, repairs, or hands off the draft, forwarding a structured packet to the next specialist. A single infrastructure-fixer pass normalizes boilerplate at the end.

flashcards.prompt: What is MARS's headline trade-off against CodeSIM on CodeContests?

choices.text: Slightly lower pass rate (0.624 vs 0.731) at roughly 3.3x lower wall-clock cost
Higher pass rate, but far more expensive to run
Identical pass rate at identical cost, but simpler to implement

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors report MARS closing most of the gap to CodeSIM while running 3.3x cheaper in wall-clock time, with substantially smaller variance in per-task token spend.
